newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kirch's DF1 suffers setback in Hamburg court.
newsitem.headline: Kirch's DF1 suffers setback in Hamburg court.

text.p: Bavarian media mogul Leo Kirch suffered another setback against his archrival, media giant Bertelsmann AG, when a German court on Wednesday refused to lift an advertising ban it slapped on Kirch's DF1 channel.

DF1, Germany's first digital pay TV broadcaster, had sought a reversal of a court injunction which prevented it from trying to attract customers outside of its home state of Bavaria, but the court said DF1's licence restricted it to Bavaria.
The injunction was issued last month in response to a law suit filed by Premiere, the German analogue pay TV channel that is owned by Bertelsmann, French pay TV group Canal Plus , and Kirch.

Acknowleging that DF1's broadcasting licence was not clear, Bavaria's media regulator last month issued a "supplementary statement" which it said would make clear that DF1 should be able to broadcast and market services nationally.
But the court did not agree.

"DF1 only has a broadcasting licence restricted to Bavaria. This cannot be made to extend nation-wide simply through an administrative act of the Bavarian State Media Agency," said a spokesman for the Hamburg state court.
A spokesman for DF1 said the broadcaster would appeal against the court's ruling and that it expected to receive a new, nation-wide licence from media regulators.
"We presume that there will be no subsequent damages to DF1," the spokesman said.
The court's decision is the latest shot to be fired in a war that has been raging between Kirch and Bertelsmann over who will dominate the fledgling pay TV industry in Germany.
While a clear setback for DF1, the ruling could improve the chances that Kirch and Bertelsmann end their pay TV dispute soon and reach a cooperation deal between Premiere and DF1.
Bertelsmann chairman Mark Woessner said recently that talks were taking place with this goal in mind.

After disagreeing with Bertelsmann and Canal Plus over basic digital TV decoder technology last year, Kirch broke off on his own and set up DF1 to compete against Premiere, the station he helped build since its start in 1993.
Kirch owns 25 percent of Premiere and has been the channel's main supplier of feature films. Bertelsmann and Canal Plus each hold 37.5 percent of the station.
Bertelsmann holds the rights to live broadcasts of German first division soccer, which has been one of the main reasons for Premiere's 1.4 million subscribers to sign on.
DF1 has signed up around 20,000 subscribers since July, far short of its goal of 200,000 by the end of 1996.

Premiere alleges that since Kirch started DF1 he has tried to give DF1 a competitive advantage by withholding feature films from Premiere and through his role as Premiere shareholder has delayed the channel's entry into digital TV.
Digital television makes it possible to broadcast more channels in CD-like quality and offer interactive programming such as pay-per-view, home shopping or access to the Internet.
But takeup of the programming has been slow in Germany because of an ongoing dispute between Kirch and the rest of the industry over the decoders.

Because Deutsche Telekom AG has not endorsed Kirch's decoder technology, DF1 cannot yet be broadcast through German cable television networks, which have more than twice as many subscribers as satellite networks.
